headline: Oil jumped nearly 4% Friday to $103 on fears the U.S. will resume strikes on Iran, and the 10-year Treasury yield climbed back to 5.00% ahead of Wednesday's Fed decision.
dateline: Monday, October 26, 2026 · closes as of Fri Oct 23

rundown.h: The Fed is expected to sit tight Wednesday.
rundown.p: CME FedWatch put the odds of a hold at Wednesday's decision at about 88% as of Monday, after September's hike to 3.75–4.00%. The bigger question is December: FedWatch showed about 71% odds of another quarter-point hike as of Friday's close. Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference is where markets will look for that signal.

rundown.h: Big Tech's spending plans face their test this week.
rundown.p: Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday after the close, and Amazon and Intel follow Thursday. Analysts expect Alphabet revenue near $127.9 billion and Amazon near $202.2 billion, with hyperscaler capex running about $800 billion this year. The season so far is strong: FactSet had Q3 S&P 500 earnings on pace for about 29.5% growth with 24% of companies reported.

rundown.h: CoreWeave's debt now trades like distressed credit.
rundown.p: The AI cloud provider's five-year credit default swaps reached 1,129bp Friday, above the 1,000bp level usually read as distressed. Morgan Stanley cut its price target to $70 and UBS to $105, and the stock slipped 2.5%. Investment-grade bond fund LQD fell 0.41% on the day, so the stress is showing up mainly in the AI borrowers, not broadly.

rundown.h: Washington quietly rolled back some Canada tariffs.
rundown.p: The administration exempted a list of Canadian goods, including blueberries, potatoes, apples and some packaging and refrigeration machinery, from the 50% duties imposed after talks broke down in late August. A White House fact sheet said new tariffs on certain valves, carpets and waste products will offset them. A separate lawsuit filed Oct 20 challenges the Canada tariffs outright.

rundown.h: Diesel costs are landing on discount retailers.
rundown.p: Wells Fargo warned Friday that high diesel prices could squeeze dollar stores, which run large truck fleets and serve price-sensitive shoppers. Dollar General fell 4.6% and Ollie's 5.3%. It's a reminder that the fuel shock works like a tax on low-income households and on any business that moves goods by truck.

dive.title: Imports just had a record month. The hangover is next.
dive.dek: Lower tariffs, a looming truce deadline and the fuel shock pulled record cargo through Southern California in September, and forecasters expect a sharp fade into winter.
body: September was a blockbuster for U.S. ports. Descartes counted 2.55 million TEU of containerized imports, up 10.3% from a year earlier and the highest September on record; the gain pushed 2026's year-to-date total above 2025's for the first time. The Port of Los Angeles handled 1.04 million TEU, its best month ever, and Long Beach moved 997,177 TEU, up 25% and also an all-time record. China came roaring back: imports from China rose 21.2% to 924,454 TEU, lifting its share to 36.3% from 34.0% in August.

Three things drove the surge. Tariffs on Chinese goods are lower than a year ago, and importers worried the U.S.-China truce would lapse this fall (it has since been extended to Jan 10, 2027). Second, the Middle East war raised fuel costs and pushed cargo off all-water routes through a drought-limited Panama Canal and toward West Coast ports with rail links. Third, retailers restocked early. LA's Gene Seroka named all three.

The catch is timing. NRF's Global Port Tracker, from Oct 8, expects imports to hold up in October (+8.5% y/y) and then slip 1% in November, with full-year 2026 volume up just 1.4% at 25.8 million TEU. Seroka expects LA's October volume near 900,000 TEU, down from 1.04 million. Gulf Coast imports already fell 14.8% in September, and Vietnam has become LA's number-two trading partner as China's share of the port's business fell to about 40% from 60%.

For warehouse owners, the lesson is to separate pulses from trend. Front-loading fills port-adjacent space fast and flatters leasing for a quarter or two, but forecast declines in November and January show how quickly it reverses. The relative winner may be Southern California: as long as diesel stays high and the canal stays shallow, rail-served West Coast gateways keep gaining share.
watch: Mid-November: LA and Long Beach October volumes, tested against Seroka's ~900,000 TEU call.
Nov 27: China's suspended ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the U.S. lapses.
Jan 10, 2027: the extended U.S.-China truce expires; watch for another front-loading wave.
dive.src: Sources: Descartes via AJOT and Container News (Oct 8); Maritime Executive (Oct 9); FreightWaves (Oct 13, 16); NRF Global Port Tracker (Oct 8); Supply Chain Dive (Sep 24); China Briefing.

items.title: October UMich sentiment: 48.0, as year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7%
items.rel: University of Michigan consumer sentiment, Oct final

chart.src: Source: University of Michigan via FRED (UMCSENT); Oct '26 from the UMich release.

body: The University of Michigan's final October sentiment index came in at 48.0, revised up from the preliminary 46.3 and above the 46.3 consensus, but a tenth below September's 48.1. It is down from 53.6 in October 2025 and sits near the record low of 44.8 set in May 2026. Trading Economics described it as the lowest level in five months.

The two halves moved in opposite directions. Current conditions fell to 46.7 from 50.9 (the preliminary 44.7 was an all-time low), driven by an 18% drop in buying conditions for durable goods. Expectations rose to 48.8 from 46.3. Year-ahead inflation expectations climbed to 4.7% from 4.6%, and long-run expectations to 3.5% from 3.4%; the long-run gauge had held at 3.3% for three months before September.
Treasury yields rose about 4bp on release day, with the 2-year at 4.69% and the 10-year at 5.00%, though the move came alongside Friday's oil jump and wasn't tied to the survey in coverage.

experts.who: Joanne Hsu, director, UMich Surveys of Consumers
experts.view: Sentiment was essentially unchanged from September, and worries about purchasing power remain the main thing shaping how consumers see the economy.

items.src: Sources: University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers (Oct 23); Trading Economics; FRED (UMCSENT); U.S. Treasury par yields.

lead.title: Qatar steps in as Houthi strikes widen the war's oil front
lead.body:
Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Sunday to support de-escalation between Washington and Iran, and oil prices eased early Monday on the news. No outcome has been announced, and Iran's Mehr News has denied that Tehran sent any offer to the U.S. or to earlier mediator Pakistan. The diplomacy follows Houthi claims of strikes Oct 22–24 on Yanbu, Rabigh, the East-West Pipeline and King Khalid Airport; the Saudi-led coalition said it shot down two missiles on Oct 24.

The Saudi pipeline matters because it is the main route around Hormuz, now carrying about 7 million barrels a day to the Red Sea. Hormuz itself is still close to shut: IMF PortWatch counted four transits on Oct 18, against a pre-crisis norm of about 85 a day.
lead.reach: Through oil and shipping costs. Brent was $114.51 early Monday (Oct 26), down 1.9%, after its highest settle since April on Friday; a VLCC from the Gulf to China cost about $1.2 million a day in early October versus about $80,000 a year earlier.

views.view: Fears of renewed hostilities have eased for now, but the relief may be short-lived, with price risks still tilted higher and post-midterm strikes not ruled out.

views.who: Fatih Birol, executive director, International Energy Agency
views.view: He sees no credible path back to normal energy markets in 2027 while Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb remain disrupted.

reading.title: Two Sigmas and a Long Way Down
reading.dek: Jeremy Grantham's bubble rule is simple: once prices stretch two standard deviations above trend, gravity has always won in the end.
body: Jeremy Grantham has spent decades as the guy at the party quietly checking where the exits are. The British-born investor, who studied economics at the University of Sheffield and earned a Harvard MBA in 1966, co-founded Boston money manager GMO, where he is chief investment strategist. His reputation rests on a few well-timed refusals: he sidestepped Japan's late-1980s mania, skipped the dot-com party, and kept his distance from the mid-2000s housing boom.

The framework behind those calls is almost boringly simple. Take an asset's long-term price trend and measure how far today's price has drifted from it in standard deviations, or "sigma." GMO calls anything two sigma above trend a bubble. Grantham admits the cutoff is arbitrary, but it is a useful line in the sand. In a purely random world, a 2-sigma move would show up about once every 44 years. Because people get carried away, GMO's data suggests it happens closer to once every 35.

Then comes the part that makes the framework bite. By GMO's count, every 2-sigma equity bubble in developed markets over the past century eventually deflated all the way back to its old trend. Not partway. All the way. A handful went further, to 3 sigma, which Grantham calls a superbubble: US stocks in 1929 and 2000, Japan in 1989, plus housing in the US in 2006 and in Japan in 1989. All five went back to trend, and the higher they climbed, the longer and more painful the trip down.

His logic has two parts. First, a higher price today means lower returns later. You can eat the cake now or slowly over the years, but not both. Second, superbubbles tend to give warning signs: prices start rising two or three times faster than normal, the most speculative stocks begin to lag while blue chips keep climbing, and investors start behaving in plainly wild ways. The exceptions GMO found, roughly a tenth of the cases, were mostly commodities and a few emerging markets, not developed-market stocks.

The catch is timing, and Grantham's critics bring it up a lot. Bubbles can stay inflated far longer than a bear's patience or a client's. His January 2022 letter put the S&P 500 near 4,700 against a trend of about 2,500. The index has since blown well past both. The framework tells you roughly where gravity is pulling. It is much worse at telling you when gravity will win.

quote.text: We humans do crazy very well indeed!
quote.src: Jeremy Grantham, GMO, "Let the Wild Rumpus Begin," January 2022

takeaways: With the S&P near 7,620, ask how far prices sit above trend, not just near records.
Narrow, AI-led leadership while speculative names lag is one of Grantham's late-bubble signs.
A 5% 10-year Treasury raises the bar that high starting prices must clear.
